title: Impacts of Static Lighting in Confined Spaces on the Circadian Parameters, Alertness, Performance and Well-Being
research_question: To understand the cumulative effects of static lighting (300 lx and 6000 K) in confined spaces on human sleep, circadian rhythm, emotion, and cognition.

participants.description: Young males (22.6 ± 1.88 years old, BMI 23.74 ± 3.32) who were university students, healthy, with normal corrected visual acuity, regular work and rest, non-smokers, and non-alcohol abusers. All subjects were from China.
participants.recruitment: Selected to reduce influence of gender and age, and to reduce individual differences through repeated-measures design. Financially compensated for participation.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Underground confined laboratory simulating an Isolated and Confined Extreme (ICE) environment. Four sleep rooms, activity room, gym, conference room, laboratory, office, machine room, lavatories, and toilets. Not affected by daylight or outdoor noise. Static lighting condition (SLC) with 300 lx horizontal illuminance on desks, 6000 K CCT, 121.38 lx average vertical illuminance at eyes, 109.45 lx melanopic EDI, and 0.21 CS. Dim light melatonin onset (DLMO) lighting condition (DLC) from 19:00 to 24:00 on Day 1 and 8, with <30 lx horizontal illuminance, 10.61 lx average vertical illuminance at eyes, 9.75 lx melanopic EDI, and 0.02 CS.

measures.instrument: Tympanic Membrane Temperature (Tty) using Braun infrared electronic ear thermometer (IRT6520)
Saliva ELISA kit from IBL International GmbH
Calculated from hourly salivary melatonin concentrations
Sleep diary and smart sleep wristbands (Huawei B4 Pro)

findings.antecedent: Static lighting condition (300 lx, 6000 K) in confined space for 1 week
findings.consequent: Subjective sleepiness (KSS scores) at 24:00 before sleep
findings.mechanism: Reduced lighting stimulation during the first and eighth nights (dim light) provided minimal stimulation, leading to consistently high KSS scores that rose the most. However, under static lighting, sleepiness before sleep decreased as the number of days increased, possibly due to adaptation or a shift in circadian rhythm.
findings.quote: KSS scores at 24:00 before sleep from the third night to the eighth night were significantly lower than that of the first day.

findings.antecedent: Static lighting condition (300 lx, 6000 K) in confined space for 8 days
findings.consequent: Subjective sleepiness (KSS score) at 24:00 before sleep
findings.mechanism: Even with a static lighting pattern, KSS scores at 24:00 showed a general decreased trend, suggesting decreased sleepiness before sleep as confinement time increased.
findings.quote: the KSS score at bedtime was still significantly lower (p = 0.021) and alertness was significantly decreased

findings.antecedent: Static lighting condition (300 lx, 6000 K) in confined space for 5 days
findings.consequent: Subjective sleepiness (KSS score) at 24:00 before sleep
findings.mechanism: The scores on the fifth day were significantly lower than the second day, indicating a decrease in sleepiness before sleep.
findings.quote: The scores on the fifth day were significantly lower than the second day (p = 0.030).

findings.antecedent: Static lighting condition (300 lx, 6000 K) in confined space for 7 days
findings.consequent: Subjective sleepiness (KSS scores) at 8:00 upon waking up
findings.mechanism: The level of sleepiness after waking up gradually increased, coinciding with the trend of a backward shift in circadian rhythm.
findings.quote: the seventh day was significantly higher than the second, fourth, fifth and sixth days.

findings.antecedent: Static lighting condition (300 lx, 6000 K) in confined space for 1 week
findings.consequent: Core body temperature (CBT) at 24:00 before sleep
findings.mechanism: The CBT at bedtime gradually increased with the number of days of confinement, indicating increased arousal levels.
findings.quote: the fifth day was significantly higher than the second day (p = 0.011).

findings.antecedent: Static lighting condition (300 lx, 6000 K) in confined space for 1 week
findings.consequent: Core body temperature (CBT) at 8:00 upon waking up
findings.mechanism: A gradual decrease in arousal levels after waking up as confined time increased, confirming a backward shift in the rhythm phase.
findings.quote: the sixth, seventh and eighth days being significantly lower than the fifth day (p < 0.05)

findings.antecedent: Static lighting condition (300 lx, 6000 K) in confined space for 6 days

findings.mechanism: A gradual decrease in arousal levels after waking up as confined time increased, confirming a backward shift in the rhythm phase.
findings.quote: the sixth day significantly lower than the second day (p = 0.005)

findings.antecedent: Static lighting condition (300 lx, 6000 K) in confined space for 8 days
findings.consequent: Core body temperature (CBT) at 8:00 upon waking up
findings.mechanism: A gradual decrease in arousal levels after waking up as confined time increased, confirming a backward shift in the rhythm phase.

mechanisms: Prolonged lack of daylight and static lighting conditions lead to a posterior shift in circadian rhythm, evidenced by delayed DLMO and changes in melatonin secretion patterns.
Inappropriate lighting stimulation during nighttime working hours suppresses melatonin, increases CBT before sleep, and reduces CBT upon waking, contributing to sleepiness and decreased arousal.

Cumulative day-by-day effects of static lighting induce a gradual deterioration in sleep quality (increased sleep latency, decreased sleep efficiency) and cognitive performance (increased reaction time and errors).
The confined environment with static lighting contributes to a gradual increase in negative emotions such as depression and anxiety, similar to 'overwintering syndrome'.
implementation_implications: Active health interventions by dynamic lighting patterns are needed in confined spaces to safeguard human health and performance.
Dynamic lighting should simulate daylight changes to help adjust people's circadian rhythms, improve performance, and enhance well-being.
Bright lighting stimulation in the morning and dim light with low melanopic EDI at night can induce forward shifting of the circadian phase.
Light rich in long waves (e.g., red light 630 nm) can be maximized at night for shift workers to improve reaction time and alertness while reducing circadian intrusion.
Lighting strategies should consider individual shifts and visual operational needs for effectiveness.

limitations: The study focused on simulating traditional static lighting, not dynamic patterns.
The sample consisted only of young males, lacking experimental data from female samples, which may influence melatonin secretion patterns.
The study did not consider the effects of light history on participants.
The age and work patterns of university students may differ from actual confined space workers.
The fixed working schedule might have limited the magnitude of the circadian phase shift.
More long-term field validation experiments are needed to obtain more authentic data and refine human experimental data for healthy lighting design.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Impacts of Static Lighting in Confined Spaces on the Circadian Parameters, Alertness, Performance and Well-Being
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The static lighting condition (SLC) in confined spaces may pose great challenges to the health of long-stay workers, inducing sleep disorders, cognitive decline, and negative emotions such as depression or anxiety. To explore human responses to the SLC (300 lx and 6000 K), 20 young subjects (22.6 ± 1.88 years old) were recruited in the underground confined lab for a week by measuring melatonin, core body temperature (CBT), subjective alertness (KSS score), sleep quality (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, PSQI), Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT), Hamilton Depression Scale (HAMD) and Self-rating Anxiety Scale (SAS). The results showed a posterior shift in circadian rhythm after 1 week of confinement, with 0.62 h delay of dim light melatonin onset (DLMO), higher melatonin concentrations in the evening, lower melatonin concentrations at midnight, a day-by-day increase in KSS and CBT at bedtime, but this decreased daily when waking up, with cumulative effects. There was a progressive increase in sleep latency, PSQI scores, response time and scores of subjective emotion scales, meaning worse sleep, performance and emotional state. Due to limited exposure to high-lighting stimuli during the daytime, the initial concentrations of melatonin increased in the evening and decreased before sleep. In confined spaces, active health interventions by dynamic lighting patterns were proposed to safeguard human health and performance.

mechanism_chain.description: Exposure to specific light characteristics activates ipRGCs, which signal to the SCN, leading to melatonin suppression and subsequent changes in circadian parameters, alertness, and performance.

steps.to_construct: Activation of intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs)

instruments_used.name: Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS)
instruments_used.description: 9-point self-report scale for current sleepiness level

instruments_used.name: Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT)
instruments_used.description: Reaction time task measuring vigilance decrement

instruments_used.name: Salivary Melatonin
instruments_used.description: Measurement of melatonin concentration in saliva samples

instruments_used.name: Actigraphy
instruments_used.description: Wrist-worn device to monitor movement and infer sleep/wake cycles

instruments_used.name: Visual Analogue Scales (VAS)
instruments_used.description: Self-report scales for various subjective states

theory_commitments.theory_name: Non-visual effects of light on circadian rhythms
theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to specific light characteristics (e.g., high CCT, sufficient illuminance) can suppress melatonin, shift circadian phase, and influence alertness and performance independently of visual perception, mediated by intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells (ipRGCs).
